title: Nothing In Here Is Plain
logline: Five rock shelters under one overhanging brow, in which not one square metre of surface was left plain, and the paint does not sit on a flat wall but rides over every swell and hollow of the rock itself — and the one thing nobody decorated is a crack in the ceiling that drips water, which is the thing people have come here for.
human_question: If the most made-beautiful room I will ever stand in still cannot tell me whether anyone here wanted anything, what exactly was I expecting to be able to see?

place.what_kind_of_place: Five open-fronted rock shelters strung along one terrace beneath the overhanging brow of a single enormous outcrop that stands on the order of a hundred and fifty metres above a dry-zone plain. The brow carries a cut groove along its whole length so that rainwater drips clear of the mouths, which is the reason anything survives inside. The shelters are entered off the terrace through a low whitewashed twentieth-century frontage, and are dim: the only light is what comes in through the doorways and window openings, and it falls away sharply towards the back wall. Inside, every available surface has been worked — sculpture in rock, brick, stucco and wood standing in ranks along the length of the rooms, gilding, and painted plaster carried over the walls and right up across the ceilings. It is a working temple with daily ritual and a resident community, one of the most visited places in the country, and it is also a strictly protected monument on which flash is prohibited. Around and below it the same outcrop carries dozens more recorded shelters, most of them empty, many with the same cut groove and with very short inscriptions in an early script beneath it.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: One thing carries it, and it is not scale. It is that the painted surface never becomes a picture plane. The rock inside is not dressed flat: it bulges, dips, folds and drops, and the plaster and the paint were laid straight over all of it, so a ruled grid of squares filled with figures arrives at a swell in the ceiling and bends across it, and a row of identical seated figures walks over a hollow and goes momentarily out of true. The image cannot be separated from the thing it is on. Alongside that there is the best close subject on the slate: the gilding and burnish catching the little light there is, a wall of figures in such close order that the eye cannot count them, and, in the largest shelter, a fissure in the ceiling that drips, with small fish painted along the wet track the water takes, and a vessel set under it inside a metal enclosure to catch what falls.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Almost nothing, and that is the film. Three things move. The light: a shaft coming in off the terrace crosses the floor and climbs the painted surfaces through an afternoon, and where it reaches, colour exists, and a metre further in it does not. The water: one drop at a time, on no schedule anyone can film, into a vessel. And the file of people, which thickens from mid-morning and is mostly feet, soles, shoulders and backs on a floor. The camera itself is the fourth thing and it moves as little as possible: this is a film of held frames and of the slowest possible tilt up a ceiling.
place.when_it_looks_best: Late afternoon, because the interiors have to be exposed on the light that comes through the openings and nothing else, and because late light reaches furthest in. The site opens early and the organised groups arrive from mid-morning, so the quiet hours are the first and the last. Full-moon observance days are the busiest and the film does not attempt them. Midday is the worst of everything: the stone underfoot is too hot for a bare-footed crew, and the light outside is too hard for the doorway frames the film depends on. Nothing in this film needs a particular season, which is unusual on the slate.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: An interior film, and the only one in the group with no drone, no vista, no golden hour and no payoff you could describe as a view. It starts on bare grey rock in hard light, walks in through a low doorway, and then does one thing for its whole length: it looks, close and slow and still, at surfaces that were not left alone. Gilded shoulders in half-light. A ceiling that bends a painted grid over its own lumps. A wall of figures too dense to count. And it ends very small, on a crack, a painted fish, a drop of water and a bowl. It resolves on its own terms — plain to not-plain and back out into the plain again — and needs no narration at all.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes the sources' actual test, which is not a test of things. The voice never says the word greed over anything in shot and never delivers a verdict on anybody who made, gilded, painted, endowed or worships in this room, because the books do not license one: their line runs on the aim, and they exempt outright what is done with faith, kindness, compassion or plain practical sense in front of it. So the film watches the most thoroughly made-beautiful room in the country and reports that it is evidence of nothing. Then it turns the one accusation the books do make in the direction it actually points — the looking at beautiful things for the relish of looking — which is not the painters' occupation. It is the camera's. And it ends where the aim is, for once, visible in the paint: the only place in the room where you can see what the decoration was for, because it follows water.

sequence.on_screen: Hard afternoon light on the terrace outside. A long held frame of the bare overhanging brow of the rock: grey, blotched, absolutely undecorated, with the cut groove running along it and dripping nothing. Then the low whitewashed doorway, and inside it a rectangle of pure black.
sequence.voice: Everything out here was left as it is. In a moment we go in, and from the doorway to the back wall, floor to ceiling, nothing was. Before that, one thing about the books this series is reading: they begin their count of the ordinary mind in exactly the world this room belongs to — things seen, heard, smelled, tasted, touched. They count fifty-four kinds of moment in it, and they are not warning us about it.

sequence.on_screen: Inside. Eyes adjust on the cut. The slowest possible tilt from a bare stone floor up a wall of ranked figures and on over the ceiling, where a ruled grid of painted squares arrives at a swell in the rock and bends across it, out of true and back.
sequence.voice: Look at what the paint is doing. It is not on a wall. There is no flat surface in here for a picture to be put on, so the picture took the shape of the rock — the grid bends where the ceiling bulges, and the row of figures goes crooked over a hollow and straightens again. You cannot lift the image off the thing. Hold on to that, because the books are about to say the opposite about minds.

sequence.on_screen: Macro, available light. The exact edge where plaster and paint run out over living stone: a boss of rock with pigment carried over its curve, a lip where the ground layer thins and the grain of the rock comes through the colour.
sequence.voice: Here is the definition, and it is a sentence worth carrying out of this room. The attaching kind of mind is the taking of a thing as good, as beautiful, as sweet. Not the thing. The taking. The books put the whole weight on the second half of that sentence, which is why a room like this cannot convict anybody of anything, and they add something a camera immediately confirms: that kind of mind never arrives with displeasure. It comes either glad or perfectly flat.

sequence.on_screen: The long shelter at its widest: sixteen standing and forty seated figures receding into the dark in one frame, gilding picking up the doorway light. Then the inscribed rock outside in the courtyard, a panel under six feet across, twenty-five ruled lines of medieval letters cut into it, shot flat in raking light and not chalked.
sequence.voice: In 1190 a king named Nissanka Malla had statues in this cave overlaid with gold, held a great offering here, recorded what it cost him, and gave the place a new name meaning golden rock cave — and then had all of that cut into stone in the twenty-five lines you are looking at. Which is the rarest thing on this whole site: a donor stating his own aim. And the books are direct about that case. Where faith, or kindness, or compassion, or plain practical sense goes in front of the spending and the providing, they say no unwholesome mind arises there at all. They do not put a ceiling on it. They do not ask for less.

sequence.on_screen: The floor. Bare feet in single file on worn stone, soles, hems, the backs of shoulders passing through a doorway shaft; nobody's face, nobody held. Then a static wide of the room with the file crossing it, and a phone screen held up in the dark, lens first.
sequence.voice: And here is the one line the same book does draw, which is not where a film like this usually puts it. On its list of the occasions when wanting is running, in among the music and the scent and the good clothes, is this: looking at beautiful things for the relish of looking. That is not the painters' trade. It is not the gilders' and it is not these feet. It is ours. It is what a camera does for a living, and we brought one.

sequence.on_screen: A painted wall in the deepest reach of the light, figures packed in close order, hundreds of them, repeating until the eye gives up; then a slow pan along the rank of seated figures, each the same, each slightly not.
sequence.voice: The books take that one wanting and set it by three dials. Glad, or flat: a pleasing thing in front of you, or one you have no opinion about. With a justifying story behind it, or with none. And rising sharply of itself, needing nobody — or needing a push, from somebody else or from a part of you talking the rest of you into it. Three dials, eight settings, and this is the important part: not one of them makes any difference to what a wall looks like.

sequence.on_screen: The smallest frames in the film. A fissure in the ceiling of the largest shelter. Small painted fish following the wet track the water takes down the rock. Then the vessel below it, inside its metal enclosure, and one drop landing.
sequence.voice: One thing in this room was never made beautiful. A crack. And look what the paint did when it got there: it did not cover it. Somebody drew fish along the way the water actually runs, so the decoration goes where the water goes. This is the only place in here where you can see what the beauty was for — because it is following something. Everything else in this room keeps its reason to itself.

sequence.on_screen: Out through the low doorway. The terrace. Bare grey rock again in the last light, the cut groove, the plain unpainted brow, and the plain below it going blue.
sequence.voice: The books cannot be made to say that a room like that is a trap, and they will not say it. Twenty-four of their fifty-four ordinary moments are the ones they file under the beautiful ones, and they mean it as a class of mind, not as a compliment about how anything looks. What they ask is never what a thing is. It is what it is for — and that is not on any surface, in there or out here. Nothing in there was plain. Nothing in there was evidence.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, the three concepts are one argument in three stages and this room is the only place on the slate where all three stages are visible at once. C004 supplies the field and the definition: the sense-sphere minds are the minds of the world of things seen and handled, fifty-four of them [C004-P:L25], thirty of which the Pradeepika files as not beautiful and twenty-four as beautiful [C004-P:L27]; the attaching is defined by the Margaya as the taking of a thing or a person to be good, beautiful, sweet [C004-M:L13], by the Pradeepika as clinging on meeting an object that is pleasing or neutral [C004-P:L41], and it never comes with displeasure — it comes glad or flat [C004-M:L15] [C004-M:L17]. Every clause of that is a clause about the mind and not one is a clause about the object, which is the film's whole permission to stand in a room of gold and painted plaster and accuse nothing. C005 then makes the test decidable, and the decision is by aim: it lists the occasions on which greed-rooted minds run — drink, gambling, bribery, dance and music and song heard for their relish, scent, fine clothes, good food, sport, the earning and guarding and spending of wealth [C005-M:L5], courtship, married affection, children and their marriages, pleasure trips [C005-M:L7] — and then turns round and exempts the same acts outright where faith, loving-kindness, compassion or practical sense leads them [C005-M:L9], cooking to quiet hunger [C005-M:L13], clothing against cold, heat and insects [C005-M:L17], and even a fine and costly garment worn to escape being looked down on [C005-M:L19]. C006 supplies the mechanism that makes the aim finally unfilmable: the three conditions that sort the eight — a pleasing object against a neutral one [C006-P:L25] [C006-P:L74], a justifying story against none [C006-P:L33], and a mind arising sharply of its own nature [C006-P:L44] against one urged on by another person or by itself [C006-M:L5]. Eight distinct moments, none of which leaves a mark on a surface. A room where every surface has been worked and the record of why survives in one cut inscription is the only site that can stage all three: the definition, the exemption, and the proof that the camera was never going to settle it.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the obvious film here is an accusation and the sources do not authorise it. Put alone, C004 reads as a suspicion of the sense world and C005's list of occasions reads as a charge sheet, and a cave of gilded figures and two thousand square metres of paint looks like the charge proved. Read properly, C005 exempts this case twice: once because acts led by faith are named as not unwholesome [C005-M:L9], and once because the digest's own reading of the list of pleasures is that music, dance and games are there on account of the enjoying mind and not because the arts are condemned. What survives the exemption is one item, and it is the item pointed at the audience and the lens: looking at beautiful things for the relish of looking [C005-M:L5]. So the pairing turns the film round. It cannot indict the painters, the gilders, the donor kings or the people crossing the floor; the only party it can honestly implicate is the one holding the camera, and even that it states rather than proves, because the aim is interior and C006's eight settings are indistinguishable on any surface. The payoff earns itself out of the same logic. In a room where nothing is plain and no reason is visible, the fish painted along a water track is the single place where the decoration demonstrably follows a purpose — the one visible aim in the building — and it is a purpose about water, not about beauty at all.

concept_links.why: The film is the concept's own territory and the concept's own definition, in a room built to test both. The sense-sphere minds are the minds of the world of things seen, heard, smelled, tasted and touched [C004-P:L25], which is what a painted, gilded, sculpted interior is made of; and the definition of the attaching that this group is about puts every word of itself on the mind rather than on the object — it is the taking of a thing as good, as beautiful, as sweet [C004-M:L13], a clinging that arises on meeting an object that is pleasing or even merely neutral [C004-P:L41], never accompanied by displeasure [C004-M:L15], and dividing first by whether the feeling is glad or flat [C004-M:L17] and then by whether it rose of itself or was prompted, by others or by oneself [C004-M:L21]. Beat 3 is that definition said out loud over the exact edge where paint runs out onto bare rock, and it is the sentence the whole film hangs from. The digest's guards are load-bearing here and two of them are honoured by omission. The Margaya lists affection and love among the names of greed [C004-M:L13]; the digest records that as a technical point about clinging, flags it as unresolved and needing an expert check, and warns that presenting it as a verdict on family love would be wrong — so no beat goes near the devotion of anybody in this building. And the Pradeepika's own contemporary moral commentary on meat, fishing, gambling, drink, weapons and other faiths' views [C004-P:L55–L69] is that author's argument rather than the taxonomy, and it is not carried, which matters more than usual in a shrine that holds images of gods from a second tradition. The digest's closing line is the film's last beat: twenty-four of the fifty-four are counted beautiful [C004-P:L27], so the sources do not treat sense life as simply bad, and a room made beautiful is not a confession.

This is the concept the row told the film to check before implying a verdict, and checked, it exempts the case. The Margaya's list of occasions is real and long [C005-M:L3] [C005-M:L5] [C005-M:L7], and it does include the enjoyment of music, dance, song, scent, fine clothes and good food. But the same passage then works the identical acts through again and sorts them by aim, and the first motive it names as exempting is faith: where faith, loving-kindness or compassion goes in front of the earning and the providing, and where practical sense and a regard for usefulness does, no unwholesome mind arises there [C005-M:L9]. Cooking to quiet hunger and sustain a life is not unwholesome [C005-M:L13] where cooking for the relish of the taste is [C005-M:L11]; clothing worn against cold, heat and insects is not [C005-M:L17] where clothing worn to be beautiful, to catch others' minds or to seem superior is [C005-M:L15]; and a fine, even costly garment prepared and worn in order to escape the contempt of onlookers is explicitly not unwholesome [C005-M:L19]. A shrine endowed, gilded and painted as an act of faith falls inside that exemption and not outside it, and beat 4 says so over the one surviving statement of a donor's own aim. The one item on the list that the film cannot shake off is [C005-M:L5]'s looking at beautiful things for the relish of looking, and beat 5 puts it where it belongs, on the audience and the lens, without putting it on any identifiable person in frame. Every does_not_transfer line in this digest bears directly on this film and is written into it. The digest forbids reading the source as a condemnation of the arts — music, dance and games are listed on account of the enjoying mind, and a film about artists must not imply otherwise — which is why no beat treats the painters or the sculptors as suspects. It forbids minimalism and self-denial as the moral, which [C005-M:L19] refuses in as many words, so no beat recommends a plainer room. It forbids collapsing everything into motive, since the source still names theft, lying and misconduct as courses of harm done through wanting [C005-M:L3]. And the digest's uncertainty about the contempt ruling [C005-M:L19] is recorded here rather than leaned on. One further use is refused outright: this digest's categories may not be used to grade real religious practice, so nothing in the film sorts, ranks or assesses anyone's worship, and the film stays on surfaces and never on a devotion. The source's remaining examples — feeding an animal for the pleasure of watching it eat as against feeding it as a kindness [C005-M:L21], and catching or keeping beautiful animals in order to look at them [C005-M:L23] — are not used, though the second is the closest thing in the digests to the film's own subject and is the reason beat 5 turns the lens on itself. The Pradeepika's extract for this concept holds only the formal list of the eight with Sinhala glosses [C005-P:L27–L42], and the film takes nothing else from it.

Kept, and narrowed to the one job it can honestly do here, which is to close the film's escape route. Beat 6 needs the three conditions and nothing more: the object met is pleasing, which brings gladness [C006-P:L25], or it is neutral, neither pleasing nor unpleasing, which leaves the flat feeling [C006-P:L74]; the mind either carries a justifying view or does not [C006-P:L33]; and it either arises sharply of its own nature with no urging, encouragement or prompting at all [C006-P:L44] or comes about through another's prompting, or through a person working up his own retreating mind [C006-M:L5]. Eight distinguishable moments, and the point of putting them over a wall of hundreds of near-identical figures is that the wall is indifferent to every one of them — which is what stops the film ending on a reading of anybody. The digest's limits are honoured strictly and one of them is the most important sentence in this record. Wrong view must not be mapped onto any community's faith in a film; in these extracts the views in question are denials of consequence and self-serving excuses [C006-P:L33], and this is a living temple that also holds images of gods from another tradition, so the film neither maps nor mentions the category over anyone's practice. The Margaya's ranking of flat wanting above glad, and of view-backed above view-free [C006-M:L19], is flagged in the digest as unexplained in the extracts and needing an expert check, so beat 6 names the dials and asserts no ranking. Prompted wanting is ranked weaker but is not excused, so the film does not offer the push as an alibi. And the Pradeepika's background conditions for each variant, which include the type of the rebirth-linking mind, are a traditional doctrinal claim the digest says needs an expert check before any film uses it; none of them appears here, and in particular nothing in this film reads a disposition off anybody.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the question the books are asking is not what you have, or how much of it, or how beautiful it is — and that this is not a soft reading of them, it is the reading they insist on. They put the whole definition on the taking rather than on the thing taken, they exempt outright what is done out of faith or kindness or plain sense, and they refuse to be turned into an argument for owning less. What is left of the accusation, once that is honestly done, is small, precise and pointed at the viewer: looking at beautiful things for the relish of looking. A viewer could leave this film having learned to stop reading other people's minds off their possessions, and having noticed that the one thing in the most decorated room in the country whose purpose is actually visible is a line of painted fish following a trickle of water.
what_must_be_real: The room as it is. No frame in this film is lit: available light through the doorways and openings is the only light, flash is prohibited on the painted surfaces and so is every substitute for it, and a frame that cannot be exposed on what is coming through the door is lost rather than lit. Nothing is cleaned, wetted, chalked, re-gilded, moved or re-hung for the camera, and no painted surface is touched. No act of worship is filmed, interrupted, restarted, arranged or waited out in frame; no offering, no recitation, no prostration, no lamp lit for the film. Nobody in the building is a subject: the people crossing the floor are feet, soles, hems and backs in a file, no face is held, no individual is followed, and no visitor or resident is asked to look at anything, react to anything, explain anything or say why they came. The resident community's permission is the condition of the whole film and is asked for in their own terms, with what the film is and where it will be seen stated plainly and more than once. The water is filmed at whatever rate it is actually falling and is never encouraged, redirected or supplemented. The inscription is filmed as it stands and is not chalked, wetted or traced. The figures of gods from another tradition that stand in these rooms are filmed as part of the room and are neither singled out, explained nor used.
position_hint: Late in the group, and after at least one of the films that show wanting as an ordinary transaction. It works as the group's turn: the film that goes looking for the accusation, finds the sources' own exemption instead, and hands what is left of the charge to the audience. Putting it early would spend the reversal before anyone needed it. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Implying a verdict on a room built to be beautiful, which is the one thing the row and the digests both forbid. C005 exempts acts led by faith, kindness, compassion or practical sense in as many words [C005-M:L9], and its digest refuses to let the list of pleasures be read as a condemnation of the arts. Any beat that lets gold, paint or scale read as a charge is wrong on the sources, not merely tactless.

Grading real religious practice with these categories. C005's digest rules it out, and the group's other petition film carries the same prohibition. Nothing in this film sorts, ranks, assesses or explains anybody's devotion, and no worship appears in frame at all.

Mapping wrong view onto anyone's faith. In these extracts the views in question are denials of consequence and self-serving excuses [C006-P:L33]; this is a living temple that also holds images of gods from a second tradition, and the category is neither applied nor mentioned over anyone's practice.

Building a pun across the translation. The Pradeepika's class name for the twenty-four is rendered 'beautiful' in the digest [C004-P:L27], and the word inside the greed definition that also comes into English as 'beautiful' [C004-M:L13] is a different word in the source. The coincidence exists in English only. Beat 8 states the class name as a class name and the film must never argue from the overlap.

Artificial light. No frame may be lit. Flash is prohibited on the painted surfaces and every workaround — panel, bounce, torch, phone light, a longer exposure obtained by holding a lamp out of frame — is prohibited with it. The film is built so that losing a frame to darkness costs it a shot and not its argument.

Consent in a single-file room. People move through these shelters in a queue they cannot step out of, which means nobody in frame can meaningfully refuse a camera; the file is therefore filmed as a file, in feet and backs, and no identifiable person appears as a character, an example or an illustration of anything.

Reading an aim off anybody, living or dead. The donor inscription records what a king did and what it cost and is used for exactly that; it is not used to establish what was in his mind, and the film says the aim is interior rather than guessing at it.

Letting the Margaya's listing of affection and love among the names of greed [C004-M:L13] touch the devotion of anyone in this building. The digest flags that classification as unresolved and needing an expert check and warns against turning it into a verdict on love.

Carrying the Pradeepika's own contemporary moral commentary [C004-P:L55–L69] into the narration. It is that author's argument rather than the taxonomy, and it includes remarks on other faiths' views, which in a shrine of two traditions would be indefensible.

Asserting the Margaya's strength ranking, which puts flat wanting above glad and view-backed above view-free [C006-M:L19]. The digest records it as unexplained in the extracts and needing an expert check. Beat 6 names the three dials and ranks nothing.

Preaching deprivation. The source allows a fine and even costly garment worn to escape contempt [C005-M:L19] and does not ask for less; a film that ends up recommending a plainer room has inverted it.

Becoming a heritage documentary. The history is the argument, not the content. The moment the voice starts explaining the phases, the dynasties and the conservation history, the film has lost its subject; the only history it needs is one donor stating his own aim in twenty-five lines.

Smoothing the figures. The statue counts, the painted area, the room dimensions, the number of statues gilded in 1190 and the date of the earliest surviving paint all differ between sources, and the differences are kept apart in the location's disputed block rather than averaged into a clean number for the narration. No count is spoken in the film.

Repeating the rock-citadel film seventeen kilometres away. That film is an ascent, a plastered wall of visitors' verses, a gateway's paws and a summit; this one is interior, has no climb in it, uses no inscription made by visitors, and has no view. The shared temptation is the painted figures in a rock shelter, and this film's painted surfaces are used for how the paint meets the rock, never for who the figures are.

Overstating the water. That the drip never ceases in drought and never overflows is what pilgrims are recorded as believing; no measurement, gauge or study was found, and the voice does not assert it.

The site's recent record includes a modern inter-communal dispute in its immediate surroundings. It is not researched into this record, is not narrated and is not filmed. It is a live grievance of identifiable people, and a group whose concepts are the greed-rooted minds cannot go near it on any framing.
drop_if: The community will not have a camera inside the shelters at all. This is a genuine possibility and the film is not attempted against it; what survives in that case is stated in the location's access note and is a different, smaller film about the terrace, the brow, the cut groove and the empty shelters around the rock, which would need its own record rather than this one's beats.
Filming inside cannot be done without holding up a single-file route past people at worship.
The only way to get an exposure on the ceiling is to add light.
The fissure, the painted fish and the vessel cannot be filmed, since the film's payoff has no second version.
Access is offered on condition that the room is presented as an example of anything, or that the film supplies a moral about devotion, wealth or offerings.

connections.note: Seventeen kilometres apart and deliberately opposite in every choice. That film is an exterior ascent in changing light with a summit at the end of it, and its painted figures are there because nobody can name them; this one never leaves an interior, never climbs, never sees a view, and its painted figures are there because of what the paint does when it meets the rock. Neither uses the other's argument and they share no shot.

The group's two cave shrines, split on purpose. That one is a floor of imported tiles and an accident of discovery, close and small; this one is saturation and scale, and the one thing it finds unpainted is a crack. Each is the other's control: a room where everything was made beautiful, and a room where the remarkable thing was brought in from somewhere else.

The slate's other rock temple in the same district, and the reason this film had to be interior. That one stays outside the shrines on principle and is carried by a single struck sound crossing a valley; this one never goes outside after its first beat and has almost no sound in it at all.

Two films about what people spent on a thing. That one is a walled town two empires held for a smell, at street level in hard coastal light; this one is one room a succession of kings kept re-gilding, in the dark. Neither narrates the spending as appetite.

selection.reason: A destination whose documented history turns on the group's own question — what an act was for — and where the sources' answer is an exemption rather than an accusation. It is also the group's only interior film and its only film with no drone, no vista and no change of light beyond what comes through a doorway.

review.note: Written fresh, not patched, and the verdict is reset accordingly. The old film went because it failed the standing standard in the specific way the reassignment brief names: a scatter of potters' households on an eastern coastal plain is an honest working place that carried the concept only by analogy — one wheel happens to make a water pot and an ornament in the same morning — and it had no chronicled, inscribed or disputed story in it at all, which is the exact mistake the rework exists to remove. Its structure also depended on filming a working household's trade and its point of sale, which in a group about the greed-rooted minds puts a camera on identifiable people at the moment they are buying and selling. The historical binding of the replacement is that this is one of the very few sites in the country where a donor's own account of his aim survives in the first person: a rock inscription in twenty-five lines of medieval Sinhala, published in Epigraphia Zeylanica I, in which Nissanka Malla records that in the late twelfth century he had the images in this cave overlaid with gold, held an offering at a stated cost, and renamed the place with a name meaning golden rock cave. The group's concepts sort acts by aim rather than by object, and here the aim is cut into stone — while everything else about the room, five shelters worked continuously from the third century BC to a repainting in 1915, keeps its reason entirely to itself. The row's central question was checked before a line was written and the answer is an exemption: C005 names faith, loving-kindness, compassion and practical sense as motives under which the same acts of providing and spending are not unwholesome [C005-M:L9], and its digest refuses to let the list of pleasures be read as a condemnation of the arts. So no beat implies a verdict on a room built to be beautiful. What does survive C005's exemption is the one item aimed at the audience — looking at beautiful things for the relish of looking [C005-M:L5] — and the film hands it to itself and its viewer rather than to the painters, the donors or anyone in frame. The guards: no artificial light anywhere, flash being prohibited and every substitute with it, so a frame that cannot be exposed on doorway light is lost and not lit; no worship filmed, interrupted, arranged or lit; nobody identifiable in frame, the file filmed as feet and backs because it cannot step out of a single-file room and so cannot refuse a camera; no verdict on the donor kings and no reading of anybody's mind; the images of gods from a second tradition filmed as part of the room and never singled out or explained, and C006's wrong view never mapped onto anyone's faith; no count spoken, because the statue totals, the painted area and the room dimensions differ irreconcilably between sources and are held apart in what_is_disputed; no pun built across the English translation of the class name for the twenty-four beautiful minds; the modern inter-communal dispute in the site's surroundings neither researched, narrated nor filmed. Separation from the rock citadel seventeen kilometres away is total by construction — interior against exterior, no ascent, no visitors' inscriptions, no summit, no view, no change of day — and the record notes that this location puts a third film in the same district, which is a slate-level judgement for Chathura rather than something this rewrite can settle. The location, title, place, two_layers, an eight-beat sequence, all three concept links, the risks, the drop conditions and the connections are all new; the previous title is kept in aliases.

suggested_location.why_here: It is the only place that hands this film both halves of the standard in the same frame. The concept turns on the difference between an act and its object, and this is a room where the object has been worked past any possible restraint — five shelters, on the order of 150 statues, something over two thousand square metres of painted plaster carried up across the ceilings — and where the reason for almost none of it survives, except in one inscription in which a donor states his own aim in the first person. That is the exact evidence C005's test needs and the exact shortage that makes the test honest. Cinematically it is the group's only interior and the slate's best available-light subject: because the rock was never dressed flat, the paint rides the swells and hollows of the ceiling and the ruled grid of squares visibly bends across them, so the film's most beautiful frame - a painted geometry taking the shape of the stone it is on - is also its clearest statement, that the image cannot be separated from the thing. And the payoff is already in the room: a fissure in the largest ceiling, small fish painted along the wet track the water takes, and a vessel underneath to catch it, which is the one surface on the site whose purpose can be seen.

historical_thread.story:
The rock stands alone on the dry-zone plain, on the order of a hundred and fifty metres above it, and its western brow overhangs far enough to keep rain off a line of shelters beneath. Somebody long ago cut a groove along the whole length of that brow so the water drips clear of the mouths, and that groove is the reason there is anything inside to film. More than eighty shelters have been recorded in and around the outcrop, and about thirty-seven of them carry very short inscriptions in early Brahmi beneath the drip-ledge, dated on letter forms to somewhere between the third century BC and the second century AD. Two of those inscriptions name royalty — one reads as Devanampiya Maharaja Gamini Tissa and one as Gamini Abhaya — and scholars have proposed Devanampiyatissa, Saddhatissa and Valagamba as the persons meant, without settling it. Three kilometres or so away, a megalithic cemetery radiocarbon-dated to roughly 750 to 400 BC has been excavated; a connection between the people buried there and the shelters is speculated and has not been shown.

The story everybody tells about the place is that Valagamba — Vattagamani Abhaya, who lost Anuradhapura to an invasion and spent fourteen years in exile — was sheltered here by the monks living in these caves, and that on regaining his throne in the first century BC he endowed the shelters as a monastery in gratitude. That account is not in the earliest record. It is carried by the Pujavaliya, the Rajavaliya and the Rajaratnakara, the last of which is an eighteenth-century work — which is to say the founding story of the place is written down in the same century as most of the paint now on its ceilings. The earliest chronicle mention of the site itself is later than the king by more than a thousand years: the Culavamsa names it, as Jambukola Vihara, in the reign of Vijayabahu I, 1055 to 1110, who is recorded as having renovated it. Rock temples in general are traditionally ascribed to Valagamba's exile, and this is one of them; the tradition is old, wide and unproven.

What is inscribed rather than traditional is a donation nine hundred years later. On rock in the courtyard, just past the entrance hall, there is a panel about five feet nine inches by three feet six, cut in twenty-five ruled lines of medieval Sinhala letters of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. It is the inscription of Kirti Nissanka Malla, who reigned 1187 to 1196, and it was edited by D. M. de Z. Wickremasinghe in Epigraphia Zeylanica volume I, pages 121 to 135. Among the king's works it records that he had the Buddha images in this cave overlaid with gold, celebrated a great offering at a cost of seven lakhs, and renamed the place Svarnagiri-guha, the golden rock cave — a name whose Sinhala descendant, Rangiri, meaning golden rock, is still attached to the site. How many images he gilded is reported as fifty in some accounts, about seventy in others and seventy-three in others again. He is also credited with commissioning the sculpture in the first shelter and with giving the caves on the terrace something close to the layout they still have.

After him the record is a sequence of restorations, and the work of each one covered the work before it. Senarath, who reigned 1604 to 1634, Vimaladharmasuriya II, 1687 to 1707, and Sri Veera Parakrama Narendrasinha, 1707 to 1739, all contributed. Under Kirti Sri Rajasinha, 1747 to 1782, the whole complex was restored and refurbished on the king's direction, and it is to this campaign and the later Kandyan kingdom generally that nearly all the visible painting belongs: the murals in the five shelters are the work of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, attributed to the Nilagama line of temple painters, and they were applied over what was there before. The technique is tempera on a dry ground: a base coat of white ceramic clay mixed with the slime of para fruit peel, rice gruel and other ingredients bound with wild bees' honey, then a top coat of white mineral clay, each left about a week, and the prepared surface ruled off with threads into a grid before any figure was drawn. Yellow came from the resin of the gokuta tree, blue from the leaves of blue avariya and bitternut ground and buried for six months, black from roasted resins emulsified with woodapple latex, red outlines from the membrane of imbul; vermilion was imported. Fragments in the third shelter have been dated to between the fifth and seventh centuries AD, which makes them, not the first-century-BC foundation, the earliest surviving paint on the site. Then in 1915 the caves were entirely repainted again, with the help of a local donor, Tolambagolle Korala of Ehelepola. The verandah facades that now close the shelter mouths were built in the 1930s. The site was declared a protected monument by gazette notification on 30 August 1957 and its sacred area on 16 April 1981, and it was inscribed on the World Heritage list in 1991. In the mid-1980s a painted stupa in the fourth shelter was broken open by thieves.

And in the second and largest shelter, water comes through a fissure in the ceiling. It falls into a vessel set inside a metal enclosure, is used in ritual, and the surplus is taken away in a channel so the room does not damp. The rock at that point slopes upward, so the water tracks along the ceiling before it drops, which is why every account of the place describes it as running uphill. Somebody painted small fish along the track the water takes. Pilgrims are recorded as holding that the drops never stop even in the worst drought, and that the source never overflows either.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
The concepts in this group sort an act by its aim and not by what it produced, and this is a site whose entire documentary record is an argument about aims that mostly cannot be recovered.

Start with what C005 actually does. It lists the occasions on which wanting runs and then exempts the same acts where faith, loving-kindness, compassion or practical sense goes in front of them [C005-M:L9]. That is not a loophole; it is the structure of the passage, which runs the same act through twice on either side of the line — food for hunger against food for relish [C005-M:L13] [C005-M:L11], clothing for cold against clothing to be admired [C005-M:L17] [C005-M:L15] — and then, at its most surprising, exempts a costly garment worn in order not to be looked down on [C005-M:L19]. Applied to this place the exemption is not a stretch: an endowment, a gilding and a painted ceiling are providing and spending, and where faith leads them the source says no unwholesome mind arises there. So the film that stands in five saturated rooms and implies a verdict is not being severe. It is being wrong about the source.

The site then does the thing no analogy can, because it holds the exception. Almost nothing here records an aim. The thirty-seven drip-ledge inscriptions are a line or two long. The founding story is a tradition written down a thousand years later and in one case in the same century as the paint. Every restoration buried the one before it, so the room is a stack of acts whose reasons are gone. And in the middle of that there is one panel, twenty-five lines, in which a king states in the first person what he did, what it cost him and what he renamed the place — the rarest object on the site and precisely the object C005's test needs. The film's fourth beat is that panel, because it is the one place where the aim is on the record rather than inferred, and even there the film reports the statement and stops: a stated aim is a statement, and the source's test is about a mind. That is the honest limit and it is the same limit the camera has.

The visible paint is where the binding goes from apt to exact. C004's definition of the attaching puts every clause on the mind — the taking of a thing as good, as beautiful, as sweet [C004-M:L13], a clinging that arises on a pleasing or even a neutral object [C004-P:L41], never with displeasure, glad or flat [C004-M:L15] [C004-M:L17] — so nothing about an object testifies. Here the object refuses to testify in the most literal way available: because the rock was never dressed flat, the paint cannot be separated from what it is on. There is no picture plane to read, no image that can be lifted off and examined. The grid was ruled onto plaster laid over lumps and hollows, so the geometry bends where the ceiling bends, and the picture is the shape of the rock. A viewer looking for evidence in a surface is looking at a surface that is inseparable from a lump of stone. C006 then closes the last gap: its three conditions produce eight distinct moments — pleasing object or neutral [C006-P:L25] [C006-P:L74], a justifying view or none [C006-P:L33], sharply of itself or urged by another or by oneself [C006-P:L44] [C006-M:L5] — and not one of the eight would leave a different mark on a wall of hundreds of near-identical figures. The room is indifferent to the whole taxonomy, which is exactly what the taxonomy says.

The last piece is the item C005 does not exempt, and the site makes it unavoidable. Among the occasions the Margaya lists is looking at beautiful things for the relish of looking [C005-M:L5]. That is not the painters' occupation and not the donors'; it is the occupation of anyone who came to see, and it is the occupation of the camera. A film about the exemption is only honest if it notices that the one thing left on the charge sheet is the thing the film itself is doing, which is why the fifth beat turns the lens round and why the film never turns it on anybody else.

And then the water, which is the payoff and the argument arriving from the side. In a room where every surface was made beautiful, one feature was left exactly as it is: a crack. It is also the feature people have come for, and they have not come for how it looks. The painters, reaching it, did not cover it — they drew fish along the track the water takes, so the decoration follows the water's route. That is the only place in the whole complex where you can see what a piece of the beauty was for, because it is visibly serving something, and what it is serving is not beauty. The most made-beautiful room in the country ends on the single surface where the aim is legible, and the aim turns out to be about water.
what_is_certain: The site is a group of five open-fronted rock shelters on one terrace beneath the overhanging brow of a single large outcrop, with a groove cut along the brow to carry rainwater clear of the mouths. It is a living Buddhist temple and a protected monument, and it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1991 under the name Golden Temple of Dambulla; the World Heritage Centre's own list page now carries it as Rangiri Dambulla Cave Temple.

UNESCO's description gives the cave monastery as having five sanctuaries, calls it the largest and best-preserved cave-temple complex in the country, states that Buddhist mural paintings cover an area of 2,100 square metres and that there are 157 statues, and describes the site as a sacred pilgrimage destination for twenty-two centuries.

The five shelters and their names, from the Sri Lankan heritage literature: Devaraja Lena, the cave of the divine king; Maharaja Lena, the cave of the great kings, the largest; Maha Alut Viharaya, the great new temple; Pacchima Viharaya, the western temple; and Devana Alut Viharaya, the second new temple, for which no proper founding detail is available and which is believed to be nineteenth-century work.

More than eighty caves have been documented in and around the outcrop. About thirty-seven cave inscriptions in early Brahmi, dated on letter forms to between the third century BC and the second century AD, have been found in association with the drip-ledged shelters. Two of them contain royal names read as Devanampiya Maharaja Gamini Tissa and Gamini Abhaya.

The earliest chronicle reference to the site is in the Culavamsa, which names it as Jambukola Vihara in the reign of Vijayabahu I (1055-1110) and records that he renovated it. The Sinhala name is understood to have been rendered into Pali as Jambukola by that chronicle's author.

A rock inscription of Kirti Nissanka Malla (reigned 1187-1196) stands on rock in the courtyard past the entrance hall, covering about 5 feet 9 inches by 3 feet 6 inches in twenty-five ruled lines of medieval Sinhala letters of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. It was edited by D. M. de Z. Wickremasinghe in Epigraphia Zeylanica volume I, pages 121-135. It records, among the king's works, that he had the Buddha images in this cave overlaid with gold, celebrated a great puja at a cost of seven lakhs, and renamed the cave Svarnagiri-guha, the golden rock cave.

Later royal patronage is recorded for Senarath (1604-1634), Vimaladharmasuriya II (1687-1707) and Sri Veera Parakrama Narendrasinha (1707-1739), and the whole complex was restored and refurbished under the direction of Kirti Sri Rajasinha (1747-1782).

The visible murals in the five shelters are overwhelmingly the work of the later Kandyan kingdom, mainly of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, attributed to the Nilagama line of temple painters, and they were applied over earlier work. The UNESCO-derived description states that all the painted surfaces within the caves were painted or overpainted in a style characteristic of the Kandy school of the late eighteenth century.

The technique is tempera on a dry ground. The rock was prepared with a base coat of white ceramic clay mixed with slime from para fruit peel and rice gruel and bound with wild bees' honey, then a top coat of white mineral clay, each dried about a week, and the prepared surface was ruled off with a grid of threads before drawing. Yellow was resin of the gokuta tree, blue was made from the leaves of blue avariya and bitternut ground and buried for six months, black from roasted resins emulsified with woodapple latex, and red outlines from the membrane of imbul; vermilion was imported from India. Vegetable dyes other than the yellow were emulsified with woodapple latex.
Painting fragments in the third shelter have been dated to a period between the fifth and seventh centuries AD.
In 1915 the caves were entirely repainted with the help of a local donor named Tolambagolle Korala of Ehelepola. The verandah facades now closing the shelter mouths were built in the 1930s.
The site was declared an archaeological protected monument by government gazette notification of 30 August 1957, and the surrounding sacred area by gazette notification of 16 April 1981.

In the second and largest shelter a vessel is placed inside an enclosure to collect water that drips through a fissure in the overhanging ceiling. The water is used in ritual, and surplus is carried away in a channel so the room is not damped. Small fish are painted along the track the water takes across the rock before it drops.

The first shelter holds a colossal reclining figure of the Buddha at the parinibbana, given as fourteen metres long, with a figure of Ananda at the feet and one of Vishnu at the head, and a Vishnu shrine is associated with the cave. The second shelter holds figures of the deities Natha, Maitreya, Upulvan and Saman together with royal figures of Valagamba and Nissanka Malla. The third holds a figure of Kirti Sri Rajasinha. The fifth holds figures of Vishnu, Kataragama and Devatha Bandara. Images from a second religious tradition are therefore part of the fabric of the shrine.
A painted stupa, the Soma-cetiya, in the fourth shelter is reported to have been damaged by thieves in the mid-1980s.

Flash photography is prohibited inside the shelters on account of the paintings. Shoes are removed at the courtyard, shoulders and knees must be covered, and the terrace is reached by a stepped climb reported at around 350 to 360 steps taking about twenty minutes. The site opens early in the morning and organised groups begin arriving from about ten. Troops of toque macaques and grey langurs range over the stairways and the terrace.
A megalithic cemetery about three kilometres from the caves has been radiocarbon-dated to roughly 750-400 BC and belongs to the island's protohistoric Early Iron Age. It is a separate site.

A modern complex stands at the foot of the rock, separate from the shelters: a three-storey Buddhist museum beneath a large gilded seated figure of the Buddha, begun in 1998 and completed and consecrated in 2001, made of concrete and brick and covered in gold.
what_is_disputed: The number of statues. UNESCO gives 157. The most widely repeated breakdown is 153 statues of the Buddha, three of Sri Lankan kings and four of gods and goddesses, which sums to 160, not 157. Other accounts say simply over 150, or a collection of 150. The Sri Lankan heritage literature's cave-by-cave counts are different again — seven in the first shelter, nearly sixty in the second, fifty-seven around the main reclining figure in the third, eleven in the fifth — which totals well short of any of the round figures. No reconciliation of these counts was found and none is attempted here. The row's note of 'on the order of 150' is in the right region but is not a figure any source states as a total.

The painted area. 2,100 square metres is the figure UNESCO and most sources give for the five shelters together, and the Sri Lankan heritage literature agrees. The Central Cultural Fund's own page attaches the same 2,100 square metres to the second shelter alone. One account gives more than 2,000 square metres over the uneven surface of five caves, and a Sri Lankan newspaper feature gives 20,000 square feet, which is about 1,860 square metres. Conversions of 2,100 square metres are printed variously as 23,000 and 22,604 square feet. The row's 'thousands of square metres' overstates it: every figure found is between about 1,860 and 2,100 square metres, that is, a little over two thousand at most, and the film speaks no figure at all.

The dimensions of the second and largest shelter. Three mutually incompatible sets are in circulation. The commonest gives about 52 metres east to west, 23 metres from entrance to back and 7 metres at its highest. The Sri Lankan heritage literature gives 122 feet long, 75 feet wide and 21 feet high near the front wall, which is about 37 by 23 by 6.4 metres. A Sri Lankan newspaper feature gives 190 feet long, 99 feet wide and about 45 feet high, which is about 58 by 30 by 14 metres. Nothing found here resolves them.

How many images Nissanka Malla gilded. Fifty, about seventy, and seventy-three are all reported. The inscription's published translation records the gilding, the cost of seven lakhs and the renaming; the number appears to come from the secondary literature rather than from the quoted text, and it was not checked against Epigraphia Zeylanica itself.
The height of the rock above the plain: 160 metres, or 520 feet, in most accounts, and 150 metres in others.

The founding. That Valagamba, Vattagamani Abhaya, sheltered in these caves during his exile and endowed them on regaining the throne in the first century BC is carried by the Pujavaliya, the Rajavaliya and the Rajaratnakara, the last an eighteenth-century work, and by wide popular tradition; the Sri Lankan heritage literature states plainly that the fact is not proven, and notes that rock temples in general are traditionally ascribed to this king's exile. The earliest chronicle mention of the site itself is in the Culavamsa, a thousand years later, under Vijayabahu I. The length of the exile is given as fourteen years in most accounts and fifteen in others. The two royal names in the early Brahmi inscriptions have been read as pointing to Devanampiyatissa, to Saddhatissa or to this king, without agreement. The film treats the founding story as tradition, states it as tradition, and does not settle it.

The date of the earliest inscription at the first shelter. It is described as a first-century Brahmi inscription over the entrance giving an account of the founding of the monastery, and separately as pre-Christian Brahmi immediately below the drip-ledge of the central cave, while the corpus as a whole is dated third century BC to second century AD and the complex's establishment is placed in the third and second centuries BC. These are not the same claim and no source consulted holds them together.

The prehistoric burials. A widely repeated line says the cave temple site contains burial sites with human skeletons about 2,700 years old. The radiocarbon-dated megalithic cemetery of that age is a separate site three kilometres away — five in some accounts — and the connection between its people and these shelters is described in the literature as speculation. This looks like a fact transferred from one site to the other and it is not used.

The water. That the drops never stop even in a severe drought, and that the source never overflows in heavy rain either, is recorded as what pilgrims believe and is repeated in tourism writing; no measurement, gauge, hydrological study or dated observation of any kind was found, so whether it runs year-round is not established. The common statement that the water flows upward against gravity is a description of the ceiling sloping upward at that point so the water tracks along it before dropping; no published study of the feature was located. Its being fed by a pool on the summit that has never dried up is asserted in travel writing and is unsourced.
The number of painted figures of the Buddha. Over 1,500 covering the ceiling of one cave is one claim; over 1,000 throughout the caves is another. Neither is attributed to a count.
The date of the modern facades. The 1930s in the Sri Lankan heritage literature; 1938, with arched colonnades and gabled entrances, in the general reference literature.

The distance to the rock citadel to the north-east, which matters only for keeping the two films apart: 17 kilometres is the straight-line figure and is what the reassignment brief gives; 19 kilometres is what the general reference literature states. Both are in use and neither is wrong for what it measures.

Uploader captions on the reference images carry figures this record does not accept, including a painted area given as 2,500 metres and a claim that the paintings were done over two thousand years ago. The visible paint is overwhelmingly seventeenth- and eighteenth-century with a further complete repainting in 1915, and the captions written into this record say what the pictures show rather than repeating what the uploaders wrote.

The orientation of the shelter mouths was not confirmed against a plan. That sunset is seen from the terrace over the plain is reported, from which the fronts appear to face broadly west and late light should reach furthest in; the film's light plan rests on that inference and it needs checking on site.

what_to_film: The bare overhanging brow outside and the groove cut along it, in hard light, held long. The film's first beat depends on the outside being completely undecorated.

The slow tilt from floor to ceiling inside the largest shelter, in one move, ending where the ruled grid of painted squares crosses a swell in the rock and goes out of true. This is the shot the film is built around and it must be obtained on doorway light alone.
Macro at the exact edge where plaster and paint run out onto living rock: a boss with pigment carried over its curve, a lip where the ground thins and the grain shows through the colour.
The long rank of standing and seated figures receding into the dark in one static frame, with gilding taking whatever light reaches it.
The rock inscription in the courtyard, flat on and in raking light, as it stands: twenty-five ruled lines, not chalked, not wetted, not traced.
A wall of figures in close order, dense enough that the eye cannot count them, and then a slow pan along a rank of near-identical seated figures.
The floor and the file: feet, soles, hems, the backs of shoulders passing through a doorway shaft. No faces, nobody held, nobody followed.
The fissure, the painted fish along the water's track, the vessel in its enclosure, and one drop landing. The smallest frames in the film and its payoff.
The shaft of light itself, crossing the floor and climbing the painted surfaces over an afternoon, as the only thing in the room that changes.
suggested_location.access: By road; the town sits on the main Kandy to Anuradhapura route and the site is signposted from it. The terrace is reached on foot by a stepped climb reported at around 350 to 360 steps, about twenty minutes, from the courtyard at the foot; shoes are removed at the courtyard and the granite underfoot is punishing at midday. The site opens early and organised groups arrive from mid-morning. Foreign visitors pay an entrance fee. This is a living temple as well as a protected monument and a World Heritage site: filming inside the shelters requires the resident community's agreement and, separately, the heritage authority's, and neither has been sought. Flash is prohibited on the painted surfaces and this record treats every other form of added light as prohibited with it. Drone is treated as prohibited outright — it is reported as restricted and as stopped on sight, and the film is built so that it never needs one. Filming inside may simply be refused. If it is, what survives is not this film: the terrace, the overhanging brow, the cut groove, the courtyard inscription and the dozens of empty drip-ledged shelters around the outcrop are all outside the shrines and would carry a different, smaller record rather than this one's beats.
suggested_location.best_time: Late afternoon, on any dry day in any season; nothing in this film depends on weather or month, which is unusual on the slate. The interiors have to be exposed on the light coming through the doorways and openings, and late light reaches furthest in; the first hour after opening is the other quiet window. Midday is unusable in both directions - the stone is too hot for a bare-footed crew and the outside light too hard for the doorway frames. Full-moon observance days are the busiest of the year and are avoided.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research by web search only, on 26 September 2026; nothing checked on the ground or against printed editions. The UNESCO list page itself returned HTTP 403 to direct fetching, so the World Heritage wording quoted here - five sanctuaries, 2,100 square metres of mural painting, 157 statues, twenty-two centuries of pilgrimage, and the statement that all the painted surfaces were painted or overpainted in the late-eighteenth-century Kandy style - comes from search indexing of that page and from sources quoting it, not from the page itself, and the ICOMOS evaluation and nomination documents could not be retrieved at all. The most careful source used is the Sri Lankan heritage literature at lankapradeepa.com, which is the only source found that separates tradition from record, and it is the basis for the thirty-seven cave inscriptions, the cave-by-cave dimensions and statue counts, the 1915 repainting, the gazette dates, the fifth shelter's undocumented origin, and the explicit statement that the Valagamba founding is not proven. The Nissanka Malla inscription's content, dimensions, script date and Epigraphia Zeylanica reference (Wickremasinghe, 1912, volume I, pages 121-135) come from the same site's page on that inscription; Epigraphia Zeylanica itself was not consulted, the twenty-five-line count and the physical measurements are as that page gives them, and the number of images gilded is not taken as settled because it varies between accounts and does not appear in the translation quoted. A Siddham database record for the inscription exists and was noted but not read. The painting technique, materials and pigments come from a 2024 Sunday Observer feature and are not cross-checked against a conservation report; that feature also gives cave dimensions and a painted area that contradict every other source, and the contradictions are recorded rather than reconciled. The claim that the paint follows the rock's own contour, which the whole film rests on, is supported by the general description that the ceilings are painted following the natural contours of the rock and that the murals spread over the uneven surface of five caves, and by the Commons photographer's own description of one reference image; it has not been confirmed from a conservation study or a survey drawing and should be checked on site before anything is committed. The painted fish along the water's track are attested twice independently - in a Commons file made by a photographer at the site and in a travel account describing painted fish decorating the dripping crack - and this is the film's payoff, so it needs confirming in person first. Whether the drip runs year-round is not established at all: the never-ceasing and never-overflowing claims are recorded as pilgrims' belief and no measurement or study was found. The megalithic cemetery three kilometres away is a separate radiocarbon-dated site and the widely repeated transfer of its 2,700-year-old burials onto the cave temple is treated as an error. Six Commons files were confirmed through action=query&titles= before their URLs were written, and seventeen were checked in total; the ones written in are the six that show what the film needs. Uploader captions on Commons carry a painted area of 2,500 metres and a two-thousand-year date for the paintings, neither of which is accepted here, and the captions in this record describe what the pictures show instead. Coordinates are those published for the cave temple, 7 degrees 51 minutes 24 seconds north, 80 degrees 38 minutes 57 seconds east; no elevation is recorded here because the figures found are for the rock's height above the plain rather than for the terrace, and those disagree. Access, community and heritage permission, whether a camera is allowed inside at all, tripod rules, and the orientation of the shelter mouths are all unverified.

unknowns: No permission of any kind has been sought or found. Filming inside a living shrine that is also a World Heritage monument needs the resident community's agreement and the heritage authority's, and either may be refused outright; everything here is a research direction.
Whether the interiors can be exposed at all on doorway light with the equipment this series uses is untested, and the entire film depends on it. No frame is to be lit.
Whether the painted fish along the water's track, the fissure and the collecting vessel can be filmed, and from what distance, is unknown. The film's payoff has no alternative.
Whether the drip runs year-round is not established in any source found, only believed.
Whether a tripod, or a stationary operator, is permissible in a room people move through in single file is unknown, and the film's held frames assume it.

This record puts a third film in one district, alongside the rock citadel seventeen kilometres north-east and the rock temple to the south. The three are separated by treatment, period and argument, but the concentration is a slate-level judgement and is flagged rather than resolved.
